config.title: Test Error Boundary

intro.title: Test Error Boundary
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple error boundary component in Angular to catch and handle errors gracefully in your application. You'll learn how to use Angular's error handling mechanisms to prevent your app from crashing when unexpected issues occur. The main technologies involved include Angular components, TypeScript, and error handling patterns. By the end, you'll have a functional error boundary that displays a user-friendly message instead of a broken interface.
intro.usecase: Error boundaries are essential in production Angular applications where unexpected errors could crash the entire user interface. In financial dashboards displaying real-time stock data, error boundaries prevent a single failing chart component from breaking the entire dashboard. Similarly, in e-commerce product listings with dynamic filters and user reviews, error boundaries isolate failures in specific sections while keeping the rest of the page functional. Testing these boundaries ensures your application gracefully handles edge cases like malformed API responses or component lifecycle errors, maintaining user trust and system stability.

objectives: Construct a custom error boundary component in Angular to catch and handle runtime errors
Configure the error boundary component to intercept errors from child components
Implement error state management within the boundary to control UI display during failures
Initialize test scenarios that trigger different types of component errors
Apply the error boundary component to wrap application components for production safety
Manulate error recovery mechanisms to restore application functionality after failures
Integrate error logging within the boundary to capture diagnostic information

steps.title: Import Component, Injectable, ErrorHandler, and TestBed from Angular core
steps.instruction: Import Component, Injectable, ErrorHandler, and TestBed from '@angular/core'.
steps.hint: Use the import statement with curly braces to bring in multiple symbols from the same module.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing multiple Angular core modules
import { Component, Injectable } from '@angular/core';
steps.seedCode: // Import Component, Injectable, ErrorHandler, and TestBed from '@angular/core'
steps.expectedOutcome: The Angular core modules needed for error handling and testing are imported.
successCriteria: Component, Injectable, ErrorHandler, and TestBed are imported from '@angular/core'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You imported some symbols, but make sure to include all four: Component, Injectable, ErrorHandler, and TestBed.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check your import statement. You need to import Component, Injectable, ErrorHandler, and TestBed from '@angular/core'.

steps.title: Create a custom ErrorHandler service
steps.instruction: Create a class named CustomErrorHandler that extends the imported ErrorHandler class and implements the handleError method.
steps.hint: Use the @Injectable() decorator above the class to make it injectable as a service in Angular.
steps.expectedOutcome: A CustomErrorHandler service class is created that extends Angular's ErrorHandler and has a placeholder handleError method.
successCriteria: The code includes a class named CustomErrorHandler decorated with @Injectable(), extending ErrorHandler, and containing a handleError method.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your class is named CustomErrorHandler, uses the @Injectable() decorator, extends ErrorHandler, and includes a handleError method.
steps.feedbackWrong: The custom error handler service wasn't created correctly. Check that you have a class named CustomErrorHandler with @Injectable(), extending ErrorHandler, and implementing handleError.

steps.title: Override handleError to log errors
steps.instruction: Inside the handleError method of your CustomErrorHandler, add a console.error() call to log the error parameter.
steps.hint: Use console.error(error) within the method body to output the error to the browser console.
steps.expectedOutcome: The handleError method will log errors to the console when invoked.
successCriteria: The handleError method contains a console.error() call that logs the error parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Ensure you've added console.error() inside the handleError method with the error parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleError method should include console.error(error) to log errors. Check the method body.

steps.title: Create a test component that throws an error
steps.instruction: Create a component named TestErrorComponent that has a method called throwError which throws a new Error when called.
steps.hint: Define a class with the @Component decorator and include a method inside that class.
steps.expectedOutcome: A TestErrorComponent class is created with a throwError method that throws an Error.
successCriteria: TestErrorComponent is defined with @Component decorator and contains a throwError method that throws new Error.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a component, but make sure it has a method that throws an Error when called.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't created correctly. Check that you used @Component and defined a method that throws an Error.

steps.title: Add a button to trigger the error
steps.instruction: In the TestErrorComponent template, add a button element with a click event that calls the error-throwing method.
steps.hint: Use the (click) event binding in Angular to call a method when the button is clicked.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example button with click handler
<button (click)="triggerError()">Trigger Error</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: The component template now includes a button that will trigger an error when clicked.
successCriteria: A button element with (click)="throwError()" is present in the TestErrorComponent template.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the button has a click event binding that calls the throwError() method.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button isn't properly configured to trigger the error. Check that you're using (click)="throwError()" in the button element.

steps.title: Configure TestBed with the custom error handler
steps.instruction: In the test setup (outside the component), use TestBed.configureTestingModule to provide CustomErrorHandler as the ErrorHandler.
steps.hint: Call TestBed.configureTestingModule with an object that has a providers array containing { provide: ErrorHandler, useClass: CustomErrorHandler }.
steps.expectedOutcome: The test module is configured to use CustomErrorHandler for error handling.
successCriteria: TestBed.configureTestingModule is called with a providers array that provides CustomErrorHandler as ErrorHandler.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're providing CustomErrorHandler as the ErrorHandler in the providers array.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. Remember to call TestBed.configureTestingModule with a providers array containing { provide: ErrorHandler, useClass: CustomErrorHandler }.

steps.title: Create and compile the testing component
steps.instruction: Use TestBed.createComponent to instantiate TestErrorComponent and call detectChanges() on the resulting fixture.
steps.hint: After TestBed.configureTestingModule, call TestBed.createComponent with TestErrorComponent as the argument, store the result in a variable, and then call detectChanges() on that fixture.
steps.expectedOutcome: The TestErrorComponent is instantiated within the testing environment and its initial change detection cycle runs.
successCriteria: TestBed.createComponent is called with TestErrorComponent, the result is stored, and detectChanges() is invoked on the fixture.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling TestBed.createComponent with TestErrorComponent and then calling detectChanges() on the returned fixture.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component wasn't properly instantiated. Use TestBed.createComponent(TestErrorComponent) and then call detectChanges() on the result.

steps.title: Trigger the error and verify it's caught
steps.instruction: In the CustomErrorHandler's handleError method, add console.error() to log the error message.
steps.hint: Inside the handleError method, call console.error() with the error parameter.
steps.expectedOutcome: The custom error handler will log errors to the console when they occur.
successCriteria: The handleError method contains a console.error() call that logs the error.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling console.error() inside the handleError method with the error parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handleError method should contain console.error() to log errors. Try adding console.error(error) inside the method.

steps.title: Test error handler injection
steps.instruction: Inject the ErrorHandler service in your test setup and assert that it's an instance of CustomErrorHandler.
steps.hint: Use TestBed.inject(ErrorHandler) to get the error handler instance, then use expect(handler).toBeInstanceOf(CustomErrorHandler) to verify it's the correct type.
steps.expectedOutcome: The test should verify that the injected error handler is indeed an instance of CustomErrorHandler, confirming dependency injection is working correctly.
successCriteria: ErrorHandler is injected using TestBed.inject() and an assertion checks it's an instance of CustomErrorHandler.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using TestBed.inject(ErrorHandler) and checking with toBeInstanceOf(CustomErrorHandler).
steps.feedbackWrong: The error handler injection or assertion isn't correct. Review how to inject services in tests and verify instance types.

steps.title: Clean up test fixtures
steps.instruction: After creating the component fixture, call fixture.destroy() to properly clean up test resources.
steps.hint: Add fixture.destroy() after your test assertions to release the component and its resources.
steps.expectedOutcome: The test fixture is properly cleaned up after execution, preventing memory leaks and ensuring test isolation.
successCriteria: fixture.destroy() is called after the component fixture is created and used.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure fixture.destroy() is called after creating and using the component fixture.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fixture cleanup is missing or incorrect. After creating the component fixture with TestBed.createComponent(), you should call fixture.destroy() to release resources.
